questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a sign of mild organophosphate or carbamate poisoning?
questions.ref: p. 80, organophosphate and carbamate symptoms sidebar
questions.why: Muscle twitching is a sign of severe poisoning.

questions.q: An applicator has used small amounts of an organophosphate for several weeks with no symptoms. After one more small exposure, they become ill soon after. What best explains this?
choices: The last exposure alone was a lethal dose
The illness cannot be related to the pesticide because the dose was small
Repeated small exposures slightly reduced cholinesterase each time, so a small additional exposure caused illness
questions.why: Small repeated exposures keep lowering cholinesterase until a small extra exposure triggers illness.

questions.q: Cholinesterase inhibition can cause only acute effects, never delayed effects.
questions.why: Cholinesterase inhibition can cause acute or delayed effects.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: Cholinesterase monitoring

p: Each person has a certain **baseline level** of cholinesterase enzyme that is considered normal for him or her.
The **blood cholinesterase test** measures the effect of exposure to organophosphate and carbamate insecticides.
A baseline must be established for each person **before** he or she begins working with cholinesterase inhibitors, or during the **off-season**.
Always conduct baseline testing during the time of year when insecticides are not being used or **at least 30 days** from the most recent exposure.
Establishing an accurate baseline value often requires that **two tests** be performed **at least 72 hours (but not more than 14 days) apart**.
If you regularly use organophosphate or carbamate insecticides, cholinesterase tests should be taken **periodically** and results compared with your baseline level.

Also, anytime you feel ill or have mild or moderate poisoning symptoms, your medical professional should conduct a blood test to evaluate your cholinesterase level and compare it with the baseline level.
The purpose of routine or emergency cholinesterase monitoring is to enable a medical professional to recognize the occurrence of excessive exposure to organophosphate and carbamate insecticides.
A **significant reduction** in your body's cholinesterase level **indicates poisoning**.
A medical professional normally suggests that the affected pesticide handler **avoid further exposure** until his or her cholinesterase level returns to normal.
A drop in cholinesterase may require you to have no exposure to these chemicals for a certain period, usually **three to five weeks**, to allow your body time to build new cholinesterase.
Medical professionals can help to establish the frequency of this testing program, which will depend on how often you use cholinesterase-inhibiting pesticides.
**Occupational and environmental medicine specialists** are most familiar with this type of testing program.
Also, because different laboratories may use slightly different methods, the **same laboratory** should be used to collect and test all samples from any one individual.

questions.q: For which class(es) of pesticides might cholinesterase monitoring be appropriate?
questions.why: Cholinesterase tests measure the effect of organophosphate and carbamate insecticides.

questions.q: Baseline cholinesterase testing should be done when insecticides are not being used, or at least how long from the most recent exposure?
questions.why: At least 30 days from the most recent exposure, or during the off-season.

questions.q: An accurate baseline often requires two tests performed how far apart?
choices: At least 24 hours but not more than 7 days
At least 72 hours but not more than 14 days
At least 14 days but not more than 30 days
At least 30 days but not more than 60 days
questions.why: Two tests at least 72 hours, but not more than 14 days, apart.

questions.q: A handler's cholinesterase level has dropped significantly. How long does the manual say they usually must avoid exposure so the body can build new cholinesterase?
questions.why: Usually three to five weeks with no exposure.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a recommendation for cholinesterase monitoring in the manual?
choices: Establish a baseline before working with cholinesterase inhibitors
Test periodically if you regularly use organophosphates or carbamates
Use a different laboratory for each test to compare methods
Get a blood test anytime you feel ill or have mild or moderate poisoning symptoms
questions.why: The same laboratory should test all samples from any one individual.

questions.q: A significant reduction in your body's cholinesterase level indicates poisoning.
questions.why: A significant drop from baseline indicates poisoning.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: First aid: get medical advice and bring the label

p: Get medical advice **immediately** if you or any of your fellow workers have unusual or unexplained symptoms that develop **within 24 hours** of a pesticide exposure.
Be alert for the early symptoms of pesticide poisoning and contact (local) effects in yourself and others.
Do not wait until you or someone else gets dangerously ill before calling a physician or going to a hospital.
It is better to be too cautious than to act too late.
To help the medical professional treat you appropriately and quickly, **take the pesticide label with you**.
Bring either a duplicate copy or the one attached to the container, or, at a minimum, the **EPA registration number** of the product.
To avoid contamination and exposure, **do not carry pesticides in the passenger space** of the vehicle.
The label is important because the medical professional needs to know the **pesticide ingredients** to determine the proper course of treatment.
It is a good idea to print off extra copies of the label from the Internet.
Place one copy in your **service vehicle** and one in your **office** in case of a medical emergency.
The illustration here shows a doctor reading a pesticide label, with the caption: Always bring the label with you when seeking medical advice for exposure symptoms.
Keep in mind that even symptoms commonly associated with certain pesticides are not always the result of pesticide exposure.
Common illnesses can cause symptoms similar to those of many frequently used pesticides.
Examples are the flu, heat exhaustion or heatstroke, pneumonia, asthma, respiratory or intestinal infections, and even a hangover.
Contact with certain plants, such as **poison oak or poison ivy**, may also produce skin effects like those resulting from pesticide exposure.
However, it is best to take every precaution.
When symptoms appear after contact with pesticides, **always seek medical attention immediately**.

questions.q: If you cannot bring the whole label to the medical professional, what does the manual say to bring at a minimum?
choices: The EPA registration number of the product
questions.why: At a minimum, bring the product's EPA registration number.

questions.q: A coworker develops unexplained symptoms 6 hours after mixing a pesticide. They want to wait and see if it gets worse. What does the manual say to do?
choices: Wait 24 hours to see if symptoms clear
Get medical advice immediately and take the pesticide label
Treat it as the flu unless symptoms become severe
Call a physician only if the coworker loses consciousness
questions.why: Get medical advice immediately for unexplained symptoms within 24 hours. Do not wait.

questions.q: You should carry the pesticide container in the passenger space of your vehicle so the doctor can see it.
questions.why: Do not carry pesticides in the passenger space. Bring the label or a copy instead.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a common illness that can cause symptoms similar to pesticide poisoning?
questions.why: The manual lists flu, heat exhaustion or heatstroke, pneumonia, asthma, infections, and a hangover.

questions.q: Why does the medical professional need the pesticide label?
questions.answer: To know the pesticide ingredients so they can determine the proper course of treatment.
questions.why: The ingredients on the label determine the treatment.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: General first aid and emergency numbers

p: **First aid** is the initial effort to assist a victim while medical help is on the way.
If you are alone with the victim, make sure he or she is **breathing** and is **no longer being exposed** to the pesticide **before you call for help**.
Protect yourself from pesticide exposure before and while giving assistance.
Make sure you wear the appropriate PPE, including a **respirator** if indicated, before assisting someone in an enclosed area.
Administer **artificial respiration** if the victim is not breathing and is not vomiting.

list: American Association of Poison Control Centers: **1-800-222-1222** (Staffed 24 hours).
Animal Poison Control Center (APCC): **1-888-426-4435**.
National Pesticide Information Center (NPIC): **1-800-858-7378**.

p: Immediate action can indeed be a life-or-death matter in a pesticide poisoning.
The **product label** is the **primary source of information**.
Follow the label's specific first aid instructions carefully.
Beyond the label, call the American Association of Poison Control Centers (**AAPCC**) or a physician for additional advice.
The AAPCC's poison help line (800-222-1222) is available **24 hours** each day.
First aid is only the first response and is **not a substitute** for professional medical help.
It is very important to get the victim to a hospital, or contact **911** for emergency response, without delay.
The following are a few key points to remember when administering first aid during a pesticide emergency.

list: If oral or dermal exposure has occurred, the first objective is usually to **rinse the exposed area with water** to dilute the pesticide and prevent absorption.
Always have a source of clean water available. In an extreme emergency, use water from a **farm pond, irrigation system, or watering trough** to rinse exposed areas and dilute the pesticide.
**Never** try to give anything by mouth to an **unconscious** person.
**Do not induce vomiting** unless the label tells you to.
If inhalation exposure has occurred, get the victim to **fresh air** immediately.
Become familiar with the proper techniques of artificial respiration. It may be necessary if a person's breathing has stopped or becomes impaired.
If first responders are likely to be directly exposed to a pesticide, be sure they wear appropriate PPE.

questions.q: According to the manual, what is the primary source of first aid information in a pesticide poisoning?
questions.why: The product label is the primary source. Follow its first aid instructions.

questions.q: You find a coworker alone, collapsed next to a spilled pesticide. Before you call for help, what does the manual say to make sure of?
choices: That the victim is breathing and is no longer being exposed to the pesticide
That the spill is cleaned up
That you have found the EPA registration number
That the victim has had something to drink
questions.why: If you are alone, check breathing and stop the exposure before calling for help.

questions.q: Which number reaches the American Association of Poison Control Centers poison help line?
Which of these is NOT one of the key first aid points in the manual?
choices: Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious person
Get the victim to fresh air after inhalation exposure
Rinse the exposed area with water after oral or dermal exposure
Always induce vomiting after a pesticide is swallowed
questions.why: Do not induce vomiting unless the label tells you to.

questions.q: In an extreme emergency, water from a farm pond, irrigation system, or watering trough can be used to rinse exposed areas.
questions.why: In an extreme emergency, water from a farm pond, irrigation system, or watering trough can rinse exposed areas and dilute the pesticide.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: NPIC, animal poisoning, and pesticide on the skin

p: In addition to the AAPCC, you can call the **National Pesticide Information Center (NPIC)**.
NPIC provides a variety of information about pesticides to anyone in the United States by phone (**800-858-7378**) or online (search for "National Pesticide Information Center").
**Post all emergency numbers** near telephones and in service vehicles used by pesticide handlers.
Pets, horses, and other livestock may also be poisoned by exposure to pesticides.
For emergency information on treating pets or livestock harmed by pesticide contamination or poisoning, call the **Animal Poison Control Center** (**888-426-4435**).
Proper hygiene helps protect the skin from pesticide exposure.
Keep an adequate **water supply** with you whenever skin exposure is possible.
Other key points:

list: **Remove all contaminated clothing** immediately.
Wash the affected area, **including the hair**, with water and soap. Rinse well.
**Showering is better than bathing** to avoid prolonged contact with pesticide residues.
Avoid **harsh scrubbing**, which could damage the skin and enhance pesticide absorption.
Gently dry the affected area and wrap it in loose cloth or a blanket, if necessary.
If the skin has **chemical burns**, cover the area loosely with a clean, soft cloth.
Do **not** use ointments, greases, powders, and other medications unless instructed to do so by a medical authority.

p: The illustration shows a worker at a sink, with the caption: Washing your hands with water and soap after using pesticides prevents skin contamination.
Wash and store contaminated clothing **separately from the family laundry**.
If clothing is contaminated with a **pesticide concentrate**, or if there is concern about getting contaminated clothing clean, it is often best to **dispose of it**.
Place the clothing in a plastic bag, seal the bag, and write the name of the pesticide on it.
Take it to a **household hazardous waste collection**.

questions.q: A client's dog walked through a freshly treated area and is drooling and shaking. Which number does the manual say to call?
choices: American Association of Poison Control Centers, 1-800-222-1222
questions.ref: p. 82, NPIC and Animal Poison Control Center
questions.why: The Animal Poison Control Center handles pets and livestock.

questions.q: Why is showering better than bathing after skin exposure?
choices: It avoids prolonged contact with pesticide residues
It is faster to dry off
questions.why: Bathing keeps you sitting in pesticide residue.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT correct first aid for pesticide on the skin?
choices: Scrub hard to remove all residue
Wash the affected area, including the hair, with water and soap
Cover chemical burns loosely with a clean, soft cloth
questions.why: Harsh scrubbing can damage the skin and enhance absorption.

questions.q: You may put ointments or powders on chemical burns from a pesticide without asking anyone.
questions.why: Do not use ointments, greases, powders, or medications unless a medical authority says to.

questions.q: Clothing is soaked with a pesticide concentrate. What does the manual say is often best to do with it?
questions.answer: Dispose of it: seal it in a plastic bag labeled with the pesticide name and take it to a household hazardous waste collection.
questions.why: Concentrate-contaminated clothing is often best disposed of at a household hazardous waste collection.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: Pesticide in the eyes and inhaled pesticide

p: Because eyes readily absorb material, **fast action** is required.
Other key points:

list: Hold the eyelid open and immediately begin gently washing the eye with **drips of clean water**.
Do not use chemicals or drugs in the wash water unless instructed to do so by a medical professional or a poison control center.
Drip the water **across, not directly into**, the eye, or use an **eyewash dispenser**.
Continuously rinse the eye for **15 minutes**.
If only one eye is affected, be careful **not to contaminate the other eye**.
Flush under the eyelid with water to remove debris.
Cover the eye with a clean piece of cloth and seek medical attention immediately.

p: The basic first aid procedure for someone who has inhaled a pesticide is to get him or her to **fresh air**.
Other key points:

list: Immediately **carry** the victim to fresh air. **Do not allow him or her to walk**.
Do not attempt to rescue someone who is in an enclosed, contaminated area **unless you are wearing appropriate PPE**.
If other people are in the area, warn them of the danger.
Have the victim **lie down** and **loosen** his or her clothing.
Keep the victim **warm and quiet**. Do not allow him or her to become chilled or overheated.
If the victim is **convulsing**, protect his or her head, turn the head to the side, and watch that breathing continues.
Do **not** attempt to insert anything into the person's mouth during a seizure.
Keep the person's **chin up** to ensure that air passages are open for breathing.
If breathing stops or is irregular, give **artificial respiration**.

questions.q: Which statement about first aid response for pesticide exposure to the eye is false?
choices: You should hold the eye open and immediately begin gently washing it.
You should drip water directly into the eye.
You should flush under the eyelid with water to remove debris.
questions.ref: p. 83, 'Pesticide in the Eyes' (Review question 8, p. 87)
questions.why: False: drip the water across, not directly into, the eye.

questions.q: What is the first thing you should do to help a victim of inhalation exposure?
choices: Get the victim to fresh air.
Have the victim lie down and loosen clothing.
questions.why: The basic first aid for inhaled pesticide is to get the victim to fresh air.

questions.q: For how long does the manual say to continuously rinse an eye exposed to pesticide?
questions.why: Continuously rinse the eye for 15 minutes.

questions.q: How should the rinse water be applied to the eye?
choices: Sprayed directly into the eye under pressure
Dripped across, not directly into, the eye
questions.why: Drip the water across the eye, or use an eyewash dispenser.

questions.q: A coworker is found dizzy in a greenhouse after a fumigation. You are wearing appropriate PPE. Which action follows the manual?
choices: Have the coworker walk out to fresh air
Give the coworker water and let them rest inside
Leave the coworker until the area is ventilated
Carry the coworker to fresh air and do not let them walk
questions.why: Immediately carry the victim to fresh air. Do not allow them to walk.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT correct first aid for someone who inhaled a pesticide?
choices: Have the victim lie down and loosen their clothing
Put something in the person's mouth during a seizure
Keep the victim warm and quiet
Keep the person's chin up so air passages stay open
questions.why: Do not insert anything into the person's mouth during a seizure.

questions.q: You should go into an enclosed, contaminated area to rescue someone even if you are not wearing PPE.
questions.why: Do not attempt the rescue unless you are wearing appropriate PPE.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: Swallowed pesticide: when not to induce vomiting

body.h: Pesticide in the Mouth or Swallowed

p: If pesticide is in someone's mouth but **has not been swallowed**, rinse the mouth with plenty of water.
Then give the victim large amounts (**up to 1 quart**) of **milk or water** to drink.
If the pesticide is swallowed, one of the most critical first aid decisions is **whether to induce vomiting**.
Induce vomiting **only if the label instructs you** to do so.
Several pesticides cause **more harm when vomited** than if they remain in the stomach.
To provide first aid for a swallowed pesticide, you must know the appropriate treatment.
The decision to induce vomiting must be made quickly and accurately. The victim's life may depend on it.

body.box: Never induce vomiting if the victim:
list: Is **unconscious** or having **convulsions**.

Has swallowed a **corrosive poison**, such as a strong alkali or acid. The material burns the throat and mouth as severely coming up as it did going down. Also, it can be aspirated into the lungs and cause more damage.

Has swallowed an **emulsifiable concentrate or oil solution** product, which is dissolved in petroleum solvents. Emulsifiable concentrates and oil solutions may be **fatal if aspirated** into the lungs during vomiting.

p: **Ipecac syrup**, used as an **emetic** for almost **50 years**, is **no longer recommended** for routine use in most poisonings.
Clinical studies have demonstrated no benefit from its use.
Ipecac works too slowly (**about 20 minutes**) in inducing vomiting and results in only about **one-third** of stomach contents being voided.

questions.q: When should you induce vomiting after a pesticide is swallowed?
choices: Only if the label instructs you to do so
Only if the victim is unconscious
Only if the product is an emulsifiable concentrate
questions.ref: p. 83, 'Pesticide in the Mouth or Swallowed'
questions.why: Induce vomiting only if the label instructs you to.

questions.q: A worker swallowed some emulsifiable concentrate. Why must you NOT induce vomiting?
choices: It is dissolved in petroleum solvents and may be fatal if aspirated into the lungs during vomiting
It is not toxic when swallowed
Vomiting will make the pesticide more water-soluble
questions.ref: p. 83, 'Pesticide in the Mouth or Swallowed'
questions.why: Emulsifiable concentrates and oil solutions may be fatal if aspirated into the lungs.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the situations where you must never induce vomiting?
choices: The victim is unconscious or having convulsions
The victim swallowed a corrosive poison such as a strong acid or alkali
The victim swallowed an oil solution product
The label instructs you to induce vomiting
questions.ref: p. 83, 'Pesticide in the Mouth or Swallowed'
questions.why: If the label tells you to induce vomiting, you follow the label.

questions.q: Ipecac syrup is recommended for routine use in most pesticide poisonings.
questions.why: Ipecac is no longer recommended: it is slow (about 20 minutes) and voids only about one-third of stomach contents.

questions.q: Pesticide is in someone's mouth but has not been swallowed. After rinsing the mouth, what does the manual say to give them, and how much?
questions.answer: Large amounts, up to 1 quart, of milk or water to drink.
questions.ref: p. 83, 'Pesticide in the Mouth or Swallowed'
questions.why: Rinse the mouth, then give up to 1 quart of milk or water.
accept: a quart of milk or water
up to a quart of milk or water
up to a quart of water or milk
a quart of water or milk

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: Inducing vomiting, activated charcoal, and antidotes

p: Induce vomiting only as a first aid measure until you can get the victim to a hospital.
Do not waste a lot of time trying to induce vomiting.
Follow these steps:

list: Make sure the victim is **kneeling forward or lying on his or her side** to prevent vomit from entering the lungs and causing additional damage.
Give the victim **at least two glasses of water** to dilute the product. Do **not** use **carbonated beverages**.
Put your **finger or the blunt end of a spoon** at the back of the throat. Do not use anything sharp or pointed. Do **not** give the victim **saltwater**.
**Collect some of the vomitus** for the doctor, who may need it for chemical analysis.

p: **Activated charcoal** is another first aid treatment that can be administered when a pesticide has been swallowed.
It acts as a magnet to **adsorb** many chemicals.
Pharmaceutical-grade activated charcoal is available from most drugstores.
Activated charcoal prepared for cleaning up pesticide spills may be substituted in an emergency.
Seek the advice of a medical professional or poison control center **before** administering activated charcoal.
Take the victim to a physician or hospital.
Only general first aid practices have been discussed here.
Contact a poison control center for more help in administering first aid.
If necessary, get the victim to a medical professional or hospital.
Take the pesticide label with you.
**Antidotes** are available for only a few classes of pesticides: **anticoagulant-type rodenticides** and **organophosphate or carbamate insecticides**.
Because antidotes can be extremely dangerous if misused, they should be prescribed and administered **only by a qualified medical professional**.
Antidotes should **never** be used to prevent poisoning.

questions.q: The label says to induce vomiting. What position should the victim be in?
choices: Sitting with the head tilted back
Kneeling forward or lying on their side
questions.why: Kneeling forward or lying on the side keeps vomit out of the lungs.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a correct step for inducing vomiting?
choices: Give at least two glasses of water
Use the blunt end of a spoon at the back of the throat
Collect some of the vomitus for the doctor
questions.why: Do not give saltwater, and do not use carbonated beverages.

questions.q: Antidotes are available for which classes of pesticides?
choices: Anticoagulant-type rodenticides and organophosphate or carbamate insecticides
questions.why: Only anticoagulant-type rodenticides and organophosphate or carbamate insecticides.

questions.q: An applicator may take an antidote before spraying to prevent poisoning.
questions.why: Antidotes should never be used to prevent poisoning, and only a qualified medical professional should give them.

questions.q: How does activated charcoal work when a pesticide has been swallowed?
questions.answer: It acts as a magnet to adsorb many chemicals.
questions.why: Activated charcoal adsorbs many chemicals. Get medical or poison control advice first.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: Heat stress

p: **Heat stress** occurs when the body cannot cope with a certain level of heat.
Heat stress may affect both pesticide handlers and other workers.
A person suffering from heat stress exhibits symptoms that **closely resemble poisoning symptoms** of some pesticides.
**PPE** worn during handling or early-entry activities **may increase the risk** of heat stress.
The protective qualities of the PPE may **restrict the evaporation of sweat**, thus impeding the body's natural cooling system.
If you are under a physician's care, consult him or her before working in hot or humid conditions.
**Vests and headbands** with special pockets for **ice packs** or other heat stress prevention devices may be worn with or beneath PPE.
These will help maintain a cool body temperature.
Caption: Avoid heat stress by taking breaks and drinking water throughout the workday.
Mild forms of heat stress make people feel ill and impair their ability to do a good job.
You may feel weak and get tired sooner than usual.
You may also be less alert and less able to use good judgment.
Severe heat stress, also known as **heatstroke**, is **life-threatening**.
The normal human body temperature ranges from about **97°F to 99°F**, with an average of **98.6°F**.
With heatstroke, body temperature may **exceed 105°F**.
Staggering, loss of consciousness, or convulsions may result.
**Lack of sweating** is a common symptom of heatstroke.

questions.q: With heatstroke, body temperature may exceed what?
questions.why: Heatstroke body temperature may exceed 105°F.

questions.q: How can PPE increase the risk of heat stress?
choices: It may restrict the evaporation of sweat, impeding the body's natural cooling system
It absorbs pesticide and releases heat
It blocks fresh air from the lungs
questions.why: PPE can trap sweat so it cannot evaporate and cool you.

questions.q: A handler in full PPE on a hot afternoon is staggering and has stopped sweating. Which condition does this most match?
questions.why: Staggering and lack of sweating are signs of heatstroke, which is life-threatening.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a sign of mild heat stress described in the manual?
questions.why: Over 105°F is heatstroke, the severe form.

questions.q: Heat stress symptoms can closely resemble the poisoning symptoms of some pesticides.
questions.why: That is why heat stress can be confused with pesticide poisoning.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: Heatstroke dangers and heat stress symptoms

p: Brain damage or even death may occur if the heatstroke victim is not cooled down very quickly.
More than **10%** of severe heat stress victims die, including young, healthy adults.
Sometimes victims remain highly sensitive to heat for months and cannot return to the same type of work.

list: Fatigue, exhaustion, or muscle weakness.
Dizziness and fainting.
Clammy or hot, dry skin.
Altered behavior: confusion, slurred speech, quarrelsome or irrational conduct.
Headache, nausea, and chills.
Severe thirst and dry mouth.
Heavy sweating. Eventually, this can progress to a complete lack of sweating as the body loses the ability to control its temperature.

p: **Act immediately** to cool down if you suspect that you may be suffering from even mild heat stress.
Drink plenty of water and take breaks in the shade throughout the workday.
In hot conditions, watch for symptoms of heat stress in other workers as well.

questions.q: Which statement about heat stress is true?
choices: Wearing extra PPE prevents heat stress.
Constricted pupils is a symptom of heatstroke.
Lack of sweat is a symptom of heatstroke.
questions.ref: pp. 84–85, 'Symptoms of Heat Stress' (Review question 10, p. 88)
questions.why: Lack of sweating is a common symptom of heatstroke.

questions.q: What percentage of severe heat stress victims die, according to the manual?
questions.why: More than 10% die, including young, healthy adults.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a heat stress symptom?
questions.why: Constricted pupils is a cholinesterase poisoning symptom, not a heat stress symptom.

questions.q: On a hot day, a coworker becomes confused, quarrelsome, and has slurred speech. What does the manual say this can be?
choices: Normal fatigue that needs no action
A sign of delayed pesticide effects only
questions.why: Confusion, slurred speech, and quarrelsome or irrational conduct are altered behavior from heat stress.

questions.q: Heavy sweating can eventually progress to a complete lack of sweating as the body loses the ability to control its temperature.
questions.why: Sweating can stop completely as temperature control fails.

questions.q: What should you do immediately if you suspect even mild heat stress?
questions.why: Act immediately to cool down, drink plenty of water, and take breaks in the shade.

sections.chapter: Chapter 5 · Pesticide Hazards and First Aid
sections.title: Chapter 5 summary

p: Pesticide risk can be summarized by the equation **hazard (risk) = toxicity x exposure**.
**Toxicity** is the capacity of the pesticide to cause either short-term (acute) or long-term (chronic) injury or illness.
**Exposure** is the means by which the pesticide gets into or onto the body.
These two factors determine the likelihood that harm, that is, hazard, will come to a person who handles pesticides.
Harmful effects of pesticides may occur at the area of local contact or after uptake into the body, that is, **systemic effects**.
Pesticides can enter the body by any of four routes: through the skin (**dermal**), eyes (**ocular**), lungs (**respiratory**), or mouth (**oral**).
Some adverse effects may occur within **24 hours** after a single, usually large, exposure. These are **acute effects**.
Others may occur many years after exposure (**delayed effects**), typically from small exposures over a long period (**chronic effects**).
Pesticide handlers can minimize exposure, and reduce risk, by following label directions, using the proper application and handling procedures, and wearing appropriate personal protective equipment.
The toxicity of a pesticide product is measured in test animals by the **LD50** and **LC50** values.
These values determine the signal word that occurs on the pesticide label.
Signal words, **DANGER-POISON, DANGER, WARNING, and CAUTION**, help the user recognize how acutely toxic the pesticide is and what precautions to take.
Remember, however, that the signal word only provides information about the **acute toxicity** of the product.
Chronic and delayed effects are often the result of different mechanisms and are not related to the substance's level of acute toxicity.
People who use pesticides routinely should have regular medical checkups to determine if they are experiencing any ill effects from pesticide use.
Regular monitoring of blood **cholinesterase** levels can determine if certain insecticides are affecting an individual before symptoms appear.
Early recognition of pesticide poisoning symptoms is the key to preventing further injury.
The label often provides important information on first aid procedures for the particular pesticide product.
Make sure a copy of the label is readily available whenever you are using pesticides.
Take the label to a medical professional if a poisoning incident occurs.

questions.q: Type the equation that summarizes pesticide risk.
questions.why: Hazard, or risk, equals toxicity times exposure.

questions.q: The signal word tells you about both the acute and the chronic toxicity of a product.
questions.why: The signal word only provides information about acute toxicity.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four routes by which pesticides enter the body?
questions.why: The four routes are skin, eyes, lungs, and mouth.

questions.q: You use organophosphate insecticides routinely. What can show whether they are affecting you before symptoms appear?
choices: Regular monitoring of blood cholinesterase levels
questions.why: Regular blood cholinesterase monitoring can detect effects before symptoms appear.
